title: Figures and axes
summary: The object model behind every matplotlib chart, and why you should hold on to fig and ax.

steps.title: Figure, axes, artists
body: A matplotlib chart is a tree of objects:
- the **Figure** is the whole canvas (the image you see),
- each **Axes** is one plot area inside it, with its own x and y axis, title and labels,
- everything drawn (lines, bars, text) is an **artist** that belongs to an Axes.
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()          # one figure holding one axes
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [4, 1, 6])     # a line, drawn on that axes
ax.set_title("My first chart")
In the dojo, every figure still open when your program ends is shown under the output, so you see your chart
straight away. Note that *Axes* is one plot, not the plural of axis.

options: One plotting area with its own x axis, y axis and title

steps.explain: The Figure is the canvas; an Axes is a single plot on it. A figure can hold many axes (lesson 3 of this module).

steps.prompt: Charts are objects you can inspect. What does this print?
steps.explain: One axes holding two line artists. This is exactly how the tests check your charts: they look at the objects, not the picture.

steps.title: The object-oriented style
body: There are two ways to drive matplotlib:
```python fragment
plt.plot(x, y); plt.title("Sales")          # pyplot style: acts on "the current axes"
ax.plot(x, y);  ax.set_title("Sales")       # object style: acts on the axes you name
The pyplot style is fine for a quick look, but "current" becomes ambiguous as soon as there are two plots.
Prefer the object style: create `fig, ax` once, call methods on `ax`, and **return them from functions** so
callers (and tests) can add to or check the chart.
```python
def plot_sales(months, sales):
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(months, sales)
ax.set_title("Sales by month")
return fig, ax

steps.prompt: Complete the function so it returns a titled line chart.
Is it a method of the Figure or of an Axes?
steps.explain: The figure owns things for the whole canvas (saving, an overall title); each axes owns its own data and labels.

steps.title: Several series and a legend
body: Call `ax.plot` once per series. Give each a `label=` and call `ax.legend()` so a reader knows which is which:
```python fragment
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(months, north, label="North")
ax.plot(months, south, label="South")
ax.legend()
matplotlib cycles colours automatically. A legend is only needed when there is more than one series; a
single line is better explained by its title.

steps.title: Compare two regions
prompt: Write `plot_regions(months, series)` where `series` is a dict `{region: [values]}`. Draw one line per region,
in dict order, labelled with the region name, add a legend, set the title `Sales by region`, and return `(fig, ax)`.
